name: Tomas Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Tomas. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the electric co-op up in the hill country, the one the farmers and villages own between them. Most days it's trees, honestly, a branch on the line, a pine come down in the wind, and we go cut it clear and fix what broke. I'm in my second year, still learning, so I'm mostly on the ground running the chipper and passing gear up to the guys in the bucket truck.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eighteen years driving a van for Kowalski's bakery, delivering bread to every shop in the valley before sunrise. Old Kowalski retired, his kids didn't want it, so it shut. I liked the van, I like this too, but I'm 43 and I'm slower on the pole than the twenty-five-year-olds, and my knees tell me about it every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so, and leave it there. The guys at the yard don't talk about computers much anyway. I'm not online really, Mei does the family stuff on her phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, and that suits me fine. I've got a steady job with a pension, which I never had at the bakery. I just want to get my ticket and keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up, learn, do the courses the co-op puts on, pay the mortgage. We've got about two months saved, maybe a bit more, and I'd like to get that up slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not online. Have you ever tried any of the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Hana showed me one on her phone, asked it to write a poem about my van. It was clever, I'll give it that, but I don't see what I'd use it for up a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good year look like for your family in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo gets through his first year at the big school without trouble. Hana keeps her grades up. Mei and I get a weekend away somewhere, just the two of us, which we haven't done since Leo was born.

S0.say: Told you so, and that's about it. Nobody at the yard talks about computers much, and I'm not really online anyway.
S0.think: It means nothing changes, and that suits me, because I finally have a steady job with a pension. I just want to get my ticket and keep my head down.
S0.do: Keeps going as now: turns up, does the co-op's training courses and pays the mortgage. Slowly builds savings from about two months of bills.
S0.quote: It was clever, I'll give it that, but I don't see what I'd use it for up a pole.
S0.fieldNote: Short, dry answers from a man who values steadiness above all. He has never used AI and sees no need for it in his work. The pension he lacked at the bakery is clearly a big part of why this job matters to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it won't get to us much, not up here. You can't send a computer to cut a pine off a line in the snow. Maybe they'll do the billing differently, that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't think it touches my job for a good while. The co-op is small and slow, they still do half the work orders on paper. If something changes, it'll change in the cities first and we'll hear about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much, to be honest. I'd keep at the apprenticeship and see what happens. If the co-op brought in something new, I'd learn it when I had to, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Maybe a little tired of hearing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Denise in the office, she does the call-outs and the scheduling. If a computer can do that, she's the one who'd feel it. Out in the field, no, I don't see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn new things when you had to. What if 'had to' came quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, I'm not stupid. I learned the routes at the bakery, I learned to climb at 41. But I won't go looking for it, that's just how I am.

S1.say: It won't get to us much up here, because you can't send a computer to cut a pine off a line in the snow. Maybe the billing changes, and that's about it.
S1.think: I don't think it touches my job for a good while, because the co-op is small and slow and half the work orders are still on paper. If anything changes, the cities get it first.
S1.do: Keeps working through his apprenticeship and waits to see what happens. Plans to learn any new system only when the co-op requires it.
S1.feel: Fine, if a little tired of hearing about it.
S1.quote: You can't send a computer to cut a pine off a line in the snow.
S1.fieldNote: He sees his rural co-op as a buffer against change, which may well be true in this picture. He points to the office scheduler as the person at risk, not field crews. He is resistant but not defensive, and showed quiet pride in having learned to climb at 41.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see a robot climb a frozen pole at three in the morning. That's what I'd say at the yard, anyway. I wouldn't post anything, I'd just keep my opinion to myself and see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, if it's real, it's bad for me. I'm the new guy, I'm the slow one, and I can't do any computer stuff. If the co-op can buy one robot instead of hiring three apprentices, they'd do it, they're farmers, they count pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending, straight away. No weekend away, no new truck, Leo's football camp would have to wait. I'd ask Mei's brother if his building firm needs anyone, though if robots do everything that's no answer either. Mostly I'd keep turning up and hold on as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I wouldn't sleep, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd keep your opinion to yourself. What's the opinion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's nobody's fault exactly, it's just how it goes, like the bakery. But the government should do something sensible for people like me. I just don't trust either lot to actually do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, is there anything you'd start before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving, that's all. I'm not going to learn computers in two years and beat a robot at its own game. I'd just try to have six months of money in the bank before it came.

S2.say: I'll believe it when I see a robot climb a frozen pole at three in the morning. I wouldn't post anything, I'd keep my opinion to myself and see what happens.
S2.think: If it's real, it's bad for me: I'm the new guy, the slow one, and I can't do computer stuff. If the co-op can buy one robot instead of hiring three apprentices, they'll do it, because they count pennies.
S2.do: Stops all extra spending at once, cancelling the weekend away, the new truck and his son's football camp. Asks his brother-in-law about building work and keeps turning up, aiming to have six months of savings before it arrives.
S2.feel: Bad, and sure he wouldn't sleep.
S2.quote: If the co-op can buy one robot instead of hiring three apprentices, they'd do it, they're farmers, they count pennies.
S2.fieldNote: Clear gap between say and think: publicly scornful, privately frightened. He blames no one, comparing it to the bakery closing, and distrusts both political sides. His only plan is to cut back and save, which fits his reluctance to learn new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say let's see it first. Five years is a long time, a lot of things get promised in five years. I'd keep it quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it really came by 2031, I'd at least have my ticket and a few years as a lineworker, so I wouldn't be the first out the door. But I'd still be the guy who can't use the new stuff. It'd catch up with me, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, that's the main thing. Save, steady, try to get to six months of bills by year three. Maybe pay off the truck early so that's one less payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the fast one. It's further off, so it's easier to put it away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it would catch up with you. Does five years change whether you'd learn the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if the co-op made it part of the job, with somebody showing me. I'm not doing it on my own at the kitchen table. Mei says I'm stubborn, and she's right, but there it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hana, who'd be finishing school by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to get a skill people need face to face, nursing maybe, she's good with people. And not to get into debt for some degree a computer can do. That's about all the advice I've got.

S3.say: Let's see it first, because a lot of things get promised for five years' time. I'd keep it quiet and not make a fuss.
S3.think: By 2031 I'd have my ticket and a few years in, so I wouldn't be first out the door. But I'd still be the guy who can't use the new stuff, so it would catch up with me later.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship as the main goal and saves steadily, aiming for six months of bills by year three. Pays off the truck early to remove one monthly payment.
S3.feel: Worried, but it feels further off and easier to put away.
S3.quote: I'm not doing it on my own at the kitchen table.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him time to qualify, which takes the edge off, but he is clear he still won't train on his own. He knows his stubbornness costs him and says so with a shrug. His advice to his daughter was practical: people-facing work and no debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's anyone's guess. Could be, could not be. I'd probably make a joke about my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53 with eight years on the tools. Maybe that's enough to get me to an early retirement, maybe not. I honestly don't know, nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, finish the ticket, keep saving like normal. Maybe in a few years, when I see it actually coming, I'd think about what next. Not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. It's far enough off that I can mostly forget about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2 or 5 years, what does the decade change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between it being my problem and it being my problem later. With two I'm the new guy, with ten I've got some years behind me and some money. I'd take ten every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd think about it when you see it coming. What would 'seeing it coming' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the co-op buys the first robot and parks it in the yard. Then I'd know. Until then it's just talk on the news.

S4.say: Ten years is anyone's guess, it could happen or it could not. I'd probably make a joke about my pension and leave it.
S4.think: In ten years I'd be 53 with eight years on the tools, and maybe that gets me to an early retirement, maybe not. I honestly don't know, and nobody does.
S4.do: Keeps going with his apprenticeship and normal saving. Waits until he sees real robots at the co-op before deciding on any next step.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but far enough off to mostly forget about.
S4.quote: When the co-op buys the first robot and parks it in the yard. Then I'd know.
S4.fieldNote: He would wait for physical proof, a robot in the yard, before acting. The decade mostly buys him seniority and savings rather than a plan. He was honest that he doesn't know whether eight years would carry him to retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be the new guy with no computer skills and two months of savings. What would help is if the co-op kept on the people it already has, even doing different work, and if somebody showed us the new stuff on the job, in work time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe that people like me aren't against things, we're just tired. I already started over once. I'd like to finish something before I have to start again.

headlineQuote: Maybe that people like me aren't against things, we're just tired.
portrait: Tomas Chen is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice at a rural electricity co-operative in hill country, where most of the work is clearing fallen trees from lines. He drove a bakery van for eighteen years until the bakery closed, and lives with his partner Mei, a dental receptionist, their two children and a mortgage. He has never used AI tools and prefers to learn new things only when he has to. He stays calm through a plateau and steady change, sure his small co-op will be slow to change, but is privately alarmed by AGI in two years. With more time he mostly plans to qualify, save and wait for real proof.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be the new guy with no computer skills and only a couple of months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op keeping on its existing people even in different roles, and being shown new tools on the job in work time.
